newsitem.title: UK: Yeltsin faces troubled 48 hours, doctors say.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces troubled 48 hours, doctors say.

text.p: The next 48 hours will be crucial in Russian President Boris Yeltsin's recovery from heart surgery, top cardiologists said on Tuesday.
Yeltsin underwent a multiple heart bypass operation earlier on Tuesday, carried out by Russian surgeon Renat Akchurin and a team from the Moscow Cardiology Research Institute.
The operation took longer than the usual three to four hours and Akchurin made clear it was extensive, leading British surgeons to predict Yeltsin's recovery will not be straightforward.

Akchurin said he had performed "much more" than the three or four bypasses that had been expected. Dr Graham Jackson, a cardiologist at London's Guy's Hospital, said that indicated Yeltsin's heart disease was very advanced.
"If you have more than four, what that is telling you is that you have extensive coronary disease," Jackson said.
"My guess is that, because there were so many done, there was an American surgeon doing them. I cannot imagine there would be anyone else who could do it than someone who was shipped in specially."
Jackson said Akchurin was clearly an experienced and competent surgeon, but did not do the volume of heart bypass operations that a top American or British surgeon would do.
In Moscow Russian authorities said foreign surgeons watched the operation on closed circuit TV and Akchurin and his team carried out the operation without any assistance from outsiders.

Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey and German doctors were seen arriving at the hospital when the operation was already well under way. Debakey later praised Akchurin, his former student, and the Russian team at a news conference.
But Jackson said: "I think they quietly slipped a crack team in." For political reasons, this would not have been publicised, he added.
Analysts in Moscow said there was no evidence to support Jackson's suggestion and given the intense media interest it was hard to see how any such manoeuvre could have been kept secret.
DeBakey, who has been more open about Yeltsin's ailments than his Moscow doctors, has specifically denied suggestions in the West that Yeltsin has liver and kidney problems.
Before the operation he mentioned thyroid problems and anaemia, which had been successfully overcome.

DeBakey was quoted by CBS News on Monday as saying Yeltsin's heart was at one point this summer only working at 20 per cent of its normal capacity, with one major artery completely blocked. After treatment this improved to nearly 50 per cent.
"So basically Yeltsin was going into this operation from the cardiac perspective with multiple risk factors and reduced heart function," Jackson said.
Dr Tony Rickard, a cardiologist at London's Royal Brompton Hospital, said Yeltsin had to pass several key milestones.

"He has passed one of them -- and that is that his own heart has taken over after a couple of hours being switched off and taken over by an artificial heart that is used during the operation," Rickard told BBC television.
"The next key stage is going to be probably later this evening when he begins to wake up and we know that his cerebral (brain) function has returned to normal.

"And after that it'll probably be tomorrow morning when he is asked to take over his own breathing. And I think by that time, say at the end of 48 hours, we'll pretty much know if this has been a complete success or not," Rickard said.
Heart bypass surgery has a high success rate, with 98 percent of patients alive a year later. But there are possible complications, especially for Yeltsin.
The surgery could cause clots, which can break off and cause a heart attack, stroke or embolism in the lung. Surgery can also lead to infections.
Or the heart may not start up again with proper, regular beating. Jackson said this could be a special risk for Yeltsin.
"The immediate danger, if the surgeon has had a hard time of it, is that a graft could fail," he said. "The operation was seven hours long so this was no ordinary operation."
He added: "The question is how bad was his heart muscle when he went into the operation? Will it pick up? How will his kidneys function?"
Jackson said if Yeltsin had an impaired liver he could face other complications.
